title_zh: 市场的疯狂（Alex Edmans）｜第 431 期
subtitle_zh: 伦敦商学院金融学教授 Alex Edmans 解读情绪、羊群行为与错误定价如何驱动市场，以及反转、价值与动量策略为何依然有效、普通投资者又该如何自处。
summary_zh: 本期 Rational Reminder（第431期）由 Benjamin Felix 与 Cameron Passmore 对话 London Business School 金融学教授 Alex Edmans（第三次做客，前两次为第192、361期），围绕其新书《The Madness of Markets》展开。Edmans 用大量研究说明情绪如何驱动市场：一个国家在世界杯被淘汰后，次日股市约下跌半个百分点（相当于英国股市150亿英镑）；天气比预期晴朗时市场表现更积极。他强调区分真实效应与伪相关（spurious correlation）、数据挖掘（data mining）的方法——样本外检验、跨运动项目与多国的稳健性（robustness），以及背后的经济逻辑。节目进而讨论投资者对旧闻的过度反应如何催生逆向投资与反转（reversal）策略，价值与动量为何在个股、国家、行业层面长期有效，以及虚幻真相效应（illusory truth effect）、显著性与注意力不足等心理机制。Edmans 给普通投资者的忠告是认清自己的优势（know your edge）：若无信息优势就投指数基金，并借分散化与股权溢价之谜（equity premium puzzle）合理提高股票占比。是一堂关于人性与市场错误定价的通识课。

turns.en: After a country is knocked out of the World Cup, the market falls by about a half a percent the next day. It makes you really think that people are just not well equipped to make important financial decisions. Sometimes you don't need unique information, all you need is patience and a longer horizon.
turns.zh: 一个国家在世界杯上被淘汰之后，第二天该国股市大约会下跌半个百分点。这真的会让你觉得，人们其实并不具备做出重要财务决策的能力。有时候你并不需要什么独家信息，你需要的只是耐心和更长的时间跨度。

turns.en: Welcome to episode 431 of the Rational Rinder Podcast. I'm Ben Felix, Chief Investment Officer at PWL Capital. I'm Cameron Passmore, Chief Executive Officer at PWL Capital. Today we are joined by Alex Edmunds, Professor of Finance at London Business School, who has previously appeared on this podcast in episodes 192 and 361.
turns.zh: 欢迎收听《理性提醒》播客（The Rational Reminder Podcast）第 431 期。我是 PWL Capital 首席投资官本·费利克斯（Ben Felix）。我是 PWL Capital 首席执行官卡梅伦·帕斯莫尔（Cameron Passmore）。今天我们请到了伦敦商学院（London Business School）金融学教授亚历克斯·埃德曼斯（Alex Edmans），他此前已经两度做客本播客，分别是第 192 期和第 361 期。

turns.en: And in addition to being such a great guest, Alex is also the author of the books, Grow the Pi, Make and Tain Lies, and his new book, The Madison Markets, came out last month. And in this conversation, we talk about why a football loss can sink a nation's stock
turns.zh: 除了是一位非常棒的嘉宾之外，Alex 还是《把蛋糕做大》（Grow the Pie）和《可能包含谎言》（May Contain Lies）的作者，他的新书《市场的疯狂》（The Madness of Markets）上个月刚刚出版。在这次对话中，我们会谈到为什么一场足球失利能够拖垮一个国家的股票

turns.en: market, why identical assets can trade at different prices, and the habits that help investors avoid the common mistakes that many of us make. Stick around to the end of here, thoughts on the conversation. But for now, let's go ahead to our talk with Alex. Alex Edmunds, welcome back to the Rational Rinder Podcast. Thanks so much, Ben.
turns.zh: 市场，为什么完全相同的资产会以不同的价格交易，以及哪些习惯能帮助投资者避开我们很多人都会犯下的常见错误。请务必听到最后，听听我们对这次对话的感想。现在，先进入我们与 Alex 的对谈。Alex Edmans，欢迎再次做客《理性提醒》播客。非常感谢，Ben。

turns.en: It's great to be back. Glad to have you back. We've got a new book out. You read a lot of books. I got to say that's quite impressive. Well, there's lots of exciting research, not just by me, but by lots of other people that I love to make this accessible to a general audience. It's a huge pleasure and a lot of fun to write them. Love it.
turns.zh: 很高兴再次来到这里。欢迎你回来。你又出新书了。你写了好多书，我得说这真的很了不起。嗯，有很多令人振奋的研究，不只是我做的，还有很多其他学者做的，我很喜欢把这些研究讲得让普通大众也能读懂。写书是极大的乐趣，也非常有意思。太好了。

turns.en: Yeah, and you do. You make the research and the information very accessible, which is really cool to see. Alex, how can a football games outcome affect a nation's stock market? This is a great question because it should not. So what you learn in any finance class is that the market is affected by fundamentals.
turns.zh: 是啊，你确实做到了。你把研究和信息讲得非常通俗易懂，这一点真的很棒。Alex，一场足球比赛的结果怎么会影响一个国家的股市呢？这是个好问题，因为按理说不该有影响。你在任何一门金融课上学到的都是：市场由基本面（fundamentals）驱动。

turns.en: So what should affect a stock price is dividends and profits and sales growth. But what research actually finds is that sentiment and emotions make a difference. And so this is why I chose to look at the effect of football or soccer results is that this is something which affects investor mood.
turns.zh: 所以，真正应该影响股价的是股息、利润和销售增长。但研究实际发现，情绪和情感同样会带来差异。这正是我选择研究足球比赛结果影响的原因——它是会影响投资者情绪的东西。

turns.en: And so what my co-authors and I found is that if you study over 1,000 soccer games after a country is knocked out of the World Cup, the market falls by about a half percent the next day, which is 15 billion pounds when applied to the UK stock market. And this is because of the effect that it has on your emotions.
turns.zh: 我和合作作者发现，在考察了 1000 多场足球比赛之后：一个国家在世界杯上被淘汰，其股市在第二天大约下跌半个百分点；放到英国股市上，这相当于 150 亿英镑。而这是因为比赛结果对你的情绪产生了影响。

turns.en: Now, some listeners might think, yeah, my mood is affected by my emotions, but I'm a professional. So when I go and trade, I will put my game face on. I will block out my emotions and I will get back to rationality. But what this research suggests is that's not possible.
turns.zh: 有些听众可能会想：好吧，我的情绪确实会受影响，但我是专业人士。所以我去交易的时候会摆出“工作面孔”，把情绪屏蔽掉，重新回到理性。但这项研究表明，这是做不到的。

turns.en: You are human and if you're human, then you are susceptible to your emotions and something like this does affect how you trade or maybe how you assess a company. Can you talk about some other unlikely things that seem to move the market? Absolutely. So whether also affects the market.
turns.zh: 你是人，只要是人，就会受情绪左右；而这类事情确实会影响你如何交易，或者你如何评估一家公司。你能谈谈其他那些看似毫不相干、却确实会左右市场的因素吗？当然可以。天气也会影响市场。

turns.en: And again, you might think, okay, a weather will affect me if I'm on holiday or if I'm a farmer when I'm working outside. But actually, this was a study which has done not only in the US, but around the world is that if it was Sonya than expected for that time of the year, then the market was more positive.
turns.zh: 你也许会想：好吧，只有当我在度假，或者我是个在户外干活的农民时，天气才会影响我。但实际上，这项研究不只在美国做过，而是在世界各地都做过，结论是：如果某个时节的天气比预期更晴朗，市场表现就更积极。

turns.en: And when it was cloudy, the market went down. So a lot of these external factors, why call them external is there should not really be any effect on profits and dividends, unless weather becomes extreme, such as a floor or really sunny conditions. They shouldn't have any effect on productivity, but it does have an effect in emotions.
turns.zh: 而如果是阴天，市场就会下跌。这类外部因素有很多——我之所以称之为“外部”，是因为它们本不应对利润和股息产生任何影响，除非天气走向极端，比如洪水或者异常酷热的晴天。它们本不该影响生产率，但确实会影响情绪。

turns.en: I've got a statistical question. And this stuff is studied. How do we know that it's an actual effect versus just a statistical anomaly? This is really important. You might wonder that this is spurious correlation or even worse data mining. So what is spurious correlation?
turns.zh: 我有个统计学上的问题。这些东西都是被研究过的。我们怎么知道这是一个真实的效应，而不只是一个统计上的假象？这一点非常重要。你可能会怀疑这是伪相关（spurious correlation），甚至更糟——是数据挖掘（data mining）。那么什么是伪相关呢？

turns.en: It's something which just happens to be a chance, platinum, the data. Data mining is if researchers go and fish for spurious correlations because you want to find something significant because then you can publish a paper around it. And you might think, well, maybe the weather people looked at loads of measures of weather
turns.zh: 就是数据中碰巧出现的某种偶然模式。数据挖掘则是研究者去“捞”伪相关，因为你想找到某个显著的结果，这样就能围绕它发一篇论文。你可能会想：也许研究天气的那些人考察了大量的天气指标，

turns.en: they could look at temperature and rainfall and snowfall and cloud cover. But what was interesting is that the people who wrote this paper, they started with an existing paper which looked at just the US and they expanded it to 20, 30 countries around the world. So they made sure that it held out of sample.
turns.zh: 他们可以考察气温、降雨量、降雪量和云量。但有意思的是，写这篇论文的人是从一篇只研究美国的既有论文出发，把它扩展到全球二三十个国家。所以他们确保了这个结论在样本外（out of sample）依然成立。

turns.en: And similarly for my football paper, we didn't just look at football. We looked at all the international sports such as cricket and rugby and basketball. So the robustness of the finding is really important. And this contrast with some findings in social science where they were not found to be robust.
turns.zh: 同样，在我那篇足球论文里，我们也不只看足球，而是考察了所有国际性运动项目，比如板球、橄榄球和篮球。所以结论的稳健性（robustness）非常重要。这与社会科学中的一些发现形成对比——那些发现后来被证明并不稳健。

turns.en: For example, I think the second most viewed TED over all time by Amy Cuddy is on the effect of power poses. If you stand with your arms aloft in a victory salute, then this apparently improves your public speaking and interview performance. But that was not replicated in other settings. So I think replications are important.
turns.zh: 举个例子，我想是有史以来观看次数第二多的 TED 演讲，是埃米·卡迪（Amy Cuddy）关于“权力姿势”（power pose）效应的那一场。如果你双臂高举、做出胜利的姿势站立，据说这能改善你的公开演讲和面试表现。但这在其他情境下没能被重复验证。所以我认为重复验证很重要。

turns.en: Another thing is just basic common sense. So does it make sense for football to affect the stock market? And this is why I wrote the paper because I saw the weather papers. I thought yes, whether does affect your emotions but an issue with the weather is it's not correlated across the country.
turns.zh: 另一点就是基本的常识。足球影响股市说得通吗？这也正是我写那篇论文的原因：我看到了那些关于天气的论文，心想，是的，天气确实会影响你的情绪，但天气有一个问题——它在全国范围内并不相关。

turns.en: So maybe it's sunny in Boston and it's cloudy in New York and it's not clear who's making the trades. But when England lose, the whole of England is upset. So one thing which matters is also just economic logic. A lot of the spurious correlation that you see such as which team wins the Super Bowl affects the stock market.
turns.zh: 也许波士顿是晴天，纽约是阴天，而到底是谁在交易并不清楚。但当英格兰队输球时，整个英格兰都会沮丧。所以另一个重要因素就是经济逻辑。你看到的很多伪相关，比如“哪支球队赢得超级碗（Super Bowl）会影响股市”，

turns.en: That is not something where there is a logical argument. Interesting. I remember we had Professor Robert Novi Markson years ago now. He has a paper on global warming sunspots and the stars with respect to the stock market performance. And he's kind of cautioning about overinterpreting, I guess, statistics.
turns.zh: 这类说法背后根本没有什么逻辑论证。有意思。我记得我们几年前请过罗伯特·诺维-马克斯（Robert Novy-Marx）教授。他有一篇论文讲全球变暖、太阳黑子和星象与股市表现的关系。他其实是在告诫大家不要过度解读统计数据。

turns.en: That was a great paper where he deliberately satirized, no, I don't mean satirized in a neck away. I think it was a very useful contribution by looking at things that should not matter for the stock market and it should not even matter for emotions. And he showed that it was correlated.
turns.zh: 那是一篇很棒的论文，他是有意做反讽——不，我不是说贬义上的反讽。我认为这是非常有价值的贡献：他去考察那些本不该影响股市、甚至本不该影响情绪的因素，然后发现它们居然是相关的。

turns.en: And so this is why you have to be very careful about data mining. And that was the motivation for the football paper. There were psychological studies that show that actually football causes deaths. People have heart attacks when their team loses and Canada suicides go up when the Montreal Canadiens are eliminated from the Stanley Cup.
turns.zh: 这就是为什么你必须对数据挖掘格外小心。而那正是那篇足球论文的动机。已有心理学研究表明，足球确实会导致死亡：自己支持的球队输球时，球迷会心脏病发作；在加拿大，当蒙特利尔加拿大人队（Montreal Canadiens）在斯坦利杯（Stanley Cup）中被淘汰时，自杀率会上升。

turns.en: Cheese. So given that prior evidence had found that sports results do affect life and death, I thought it was plausible to look at the effect on the stock market. Yeah, that's super interesting. Can you talk about what the wisdom of crowds logic suggests about market prices?
turns.zh: 所以，既然已有证据表明体育比赛结果确实关乎生死，我就觉得去研究它对股市的影响是说得通的。是的，这太有意思了。你能谈谈“群体的智慧”这一逻辑对市场价格意味着什么吗？

turns.en: The main book that mine goes against is a famous one called The Wisdom of Crowds by James Terri Wickham, what he argued is that crowds actually do get to the right price. Why? Because while people might make mistakes, it argued that these mistakes might go in opposite direction.
turns.zh: 我这本书主要针对的一本名著是《群体的智慧》（The Wisdom of Crowds），作者是詹姆斯·索罗维基（James Surowiecki）。他的论点是：群体其实能够得出正确的价格。为什么呢？因为虽然人们会犯错，但他认为这些错误可能朝相反的方向发生。

turns.en: So let's say I was an Elon Musk fanboy, I'm going to be buying too much Tesla and maybe you don't like his politics and so you're going to be selling too much. We'll cancel each other out and Tesla will be fairly priced. However, when you look at the stock market, often people will be reacting in the same direction. Why?
turns.zh: 比方说，如果我是埃隆·马斯克（Elon Musk）的粉丝，我就会买入过多特斯拉（Tesla）；而也许你不喜欢他的政治立场，于是你会卖出过多。两者互相抵消，特斯拉就会定价合理。然而，当你观察股市时，人们往往朝同一个方向反应。为什么呢？

turns.en: Because human emotion goes in the same way. So lots of people might get really excited right now in artificial intelligence, fear of missing out, maybe when crypto came on the scene, people got overly excited about that before that we have the tech bubble.
turns.zh: 因为人类的情绪是朝同一个方向走的。所以此刻很多人可能会对人工智能极度兴奋，产生错失恐惧（FOMO，fear of missing out）；也许当年加密货币出现时，人们也对它过度兴奋；再往前，我们有互联网泡沫。

turns.en: And so what we have is herd behavior and that I think leads to the madness of crowds rather than the wisdom of crowds is when you have something where there is some psychological sentiment, which might be driving it, then often the crowd will all react in one way rather than canceling each other out. So interesting.
turns.zh: 所以我们看到的是羊群行为（herd behaviour），我认为这导致的是“群体的疯狂”而非“群体的智慧”。当某样东西背后存在某种心理情绪在推动时，群体往往会朝同一个方向反应，而不是相互抵消。很有意思。

turns.en: So we've done experiments with groups of people in the past to test the wisdom of crowds idea. We've given them a big jar of jelly beans in a room and we have, I don't know, maybe 50 to 100 people. Everyone casts a guess at how many jelly beans are in the jar and it's been remarkably consistent how close the average guess is.
turns.zh: 我们过去也做过群体实验来检验“群体的智慧”这个想法。我们在一个房间里放一大罐吉利豆（jelly beans），找来——我不知道——大概 50 到 100 个人。每个人都猜一下罐子里有多少颗吉利豆，而平均猜测值有多接近真实答案，其一致性令人惊叹。

turns.en: Why do you think wisdom of crowds works with jelly beans, but not in financial markets? Really good point, it's because nobody really gets emotionally attached to the number of jelly beans in a jar. So some people will guess too high and some people will guess too low and this will
turns.zh: 你觉得为什么“群体的智慧”在吉利豆上灵验，在金融市场却不灵？非常好的问题，这是因为没有人真的会对罐子里吉利豆的数量产生情感依附。所以有些人会猜得太高，有些人会猜得太低，这些偏差会

turns.en: even out, but when we think about the stock market, these are things which are affected by emotion. So lots of people will get excited by AR. There will be fear of missing out in cryptocurrency and non-fungible tokens. And so when you have something where there will be sentiment, often that sentiment will be acting in the same way.
turns.zh: 相互抵消。但当我们想到股市时，这些都是会被情绪左右的东西。所以很多人会因为 AI 而兴奋，会在加密货币和非同质化代币（NFT）上产生错失恐惧。因此，当某样东西存在情绪因素时，这种情绪往往是朝同一个方向作用的。

turns.en: Also, when you guess about jelly beans, you will often guess in secret. Whereas with trading, you know what other people are doing. Maybe your friends are telling you they've got into crypto, maybe you log on to Reddit, the Wall Street Bat sub for them.
turns.zh: 另外，猜吉利豆时你通常是私下猜测。而交易时，你知道其他人在做什么。也许你的朋友告诉你他们进场买了加密货币，也许你登录 Reddit 的 r/WallStreetBets 版块，

turns.en: You see lots of other people getting into crypto and therefore you think if I'm missing out, then I'm going to be looking foolish for not being into this new asset. And so I think that is really key. There's experiments by a Solomon Ash on conformity where he takes a standard line and
turns.zh: 看到很多人都在买加密货币，于是你想：如果我错过了，那我就会因为没有参与这个新资产而显得很蠢。所以我认为这一点非常关键。所罗门·阿希（Solomon Asch）做过关于从众（conformity）的实验，他拿出一条标准线段，

turns.en: it gives you three lines and after which of those three lines is similar in length to this standard line and what he did is he put some fake people in the audience to clearly give the wrong answer and people would follow the answer even though it should have been clear to their own eyes what the right answer is.
turns.zh: 再给你三条线段，问你哪一条与这条标准线段长度相近。他的做法是在受试者中安插一些“假受试者”，让他们明显给出错误答案，结果人们会跟着给出那个答案，尽管凭自己的眼睛明明能看出正确答案是什么。

turns.en: And so this is why listening to other people conformity can be very powerful and this is what you might get on a Reddit sub for them. Interesting. We have made the guesses private when we've done that experiment. So what types of errors do investors make? Unfortunately too many, but to let me just go with a couple.
turns.zh: 很有意思。我们做那个实验时，是让每个人私下猜测的。那么投资者会犯哪些类型的错误？遗憾的是，太多了，不过我就举几个吧。

turns.en: So one of them will be over reaction. That is the example that I gave with football is you react to something which should not really have any effect on stock prices. Now, not only can you react to something which is irrelevant, it could be that there is something which is relevant, but you still respond to it too much.
turns.zh: 其中一个是过度反应（overreaction）。这就是我举的足球那个例子：你会对一个本不该对股价产生任何影响的东西做出反应。而且，你不仅可能对本不相关的东西做出反应，也可能某件事确实相关，但你的反应依然过头了。

turns.en: For example, in the pandemic, zoom went up by 700% and clearly the pandemic was good for zoo, but to go up 700% well, people did not realize that maybe Microsoft teams and Google meet would catch up. Maybe the world will open up in a couple of years time and people would realize that they
turns.zh: 例如疫情期间，Zoom 上涨了 700%。显然疫情对 Zoom 是利好，但涨 700% 就过分了——人们没有意识到，微软 Teams 和 Google Meet 也许会追上来；也许再过几年世界重新开放，人们会发现自己

turns.en: like human interaction and they don't want to have any more online conferences, but because people are just sitting in their lockdown offices, they might not have been able to see the world going back to normal and so they've over acted in those cases.

And this is crazy because they have no expertise in moving into AI, yet the stock price went
turns.zh: 有时你会看到对纯粹的炒作、毫无实质的东西的过度反应。今年 4 月，Allbirds 这家运动鞋公司把自己重塑为 NewBird AI，宣称要转型做人工智能。这很荒谬，因为他们在进军 AI 方面毫无专长，然而股价却

turns.en: up by 582% because anything which has an AI label attached to it was heavily lauded. And so here was again another example where people react to something which is flashy and attention grabbing, not really seeing does the company have the ability to actually execute this new strategy.
turns.zh: 上涨了 582%，因为任何贴上 AI 标签的东西都会受到热烈追捧。所以这又是一个例子：人们对浮夸、抓眼球的东西做出反应，却没有真正去看这家公司是否有能力执行这个新战略。

turns.en: And why I think over reaction is so pervasive and why I think this is the headline example I'm going to give even though there's lots of errors that investors make is we see this and so many other areas of life. So if you go to any football stadium at the weekend, if the managers lost three games in
turns.zh: 我认为过度反应之所以如此普遍——这也是我要重点举的例子，尽管投资者会犯很多种错误——是因为我们在生活的其他许多领域也能看到它。周末你随便去哪个足球场，如果主教练连输了三场，

turns.en: a row, people will call for him to be fired, even if he's had four great seasons, maybe at work, if you get missed off an email or excluded from a meeting, you think, let me try and quit this company. But if you go on a date, your date doesn't show up, you might think dating is pointless.
turns.zh: 球迷们就会要求解雇他，哪怕他此前带出过四个出色的赛季。也许在工作上，如果你被漏掉在一封邮件之外，或者没被邀请参加某个会议，你会想：我该辞掉这份工作。而如果你去约会，对方没出现，你可能会觉得约会毫无意义。

turns.en: So in all of these situations, we might react to small bits of information and that's why it's very difficult to shake when you get to the stock market. You give examples of sort of overreaction to positive information where people are getting really excited. What about the other direction?
turns.zh: 在所有这些情境中，我们都会对一点点信息做出反应，这也是为什么到了股市，这种毛病很难改掉。你举的是对利好信息过度反应、人们变得非常兴奋的例子。那反方向呢？

turns.en: So people could overreact a negative information as well. So you have overreaction both the upside and the downside, just like I gave the example of not being including on an email or being excluded from a meeting. In both directions, we will have overreaction.
turns.zh: 人们同样会对负面信息过度反应。所以上涨和下跌两个方向都会有过度反应，就像我举的“被漏掉在邮件之外”或者“没被邀请参加会议”的例子一样。两个方向上我们都会过度反应。

turns.en: And so this is why then this gives rise to a contrarian investment strategy, is that if we were to sort all stocks by how they did over the last three years, look at the ones that did really well and call them the winners. Look at the ones that did really badly and call them the losers.
turns.zh: 这也正是逆向投资策略（contrarian investment strategy）产生的原因：如果我们把所有股票按过去三年的表现排序，把表现非常好的那批称为“赢家”，把表现非常差的那批称为“输家”，

turns.en: If we buy the past losers and sell the past winners and hold them for another few years, then what we see is that there is a reversal, past losers become winners and past winners become losers, so we see the overreaction in both directions. What about underreaction to investors ever underreact? They do.
turns.zh: 然后买入过去的输家、卖出过去的赢家，再持有几年，我们就会看到一种反转（reversal）：过去的输家变成赢家，过去的赢家变成输家。所以两个方向上都能看到过度反应。那反应不足（underreaction）呢？投资者会有反应不足的时候吗？确实会。

turns.en: So they underreact a different types of information. So we see overreaction to some salient, flashy news such as an AI rebrand or the fact that we're in a lockdown. Underreaction might be to some quieter things that really affect long-term value, but which the market might not realize. So one of my own studies looks at corporate culture.
turns.zh: 他们会对不同类型的信息反应不足。我们看到对某些显著、抢眼的新闻会过度反应，比如 AI 改名，或者我们正处在封城之中。反应不足则可能发生在一些更安静、真正影响长期价值、但市场没有意识到的事情上。我自己的一项研究就考察了企业文化。

turns.en: Many people will think it's quite logical that corporate culture matters because human capital is your most important asset. turns.zh: 很多人会觉得企业文化重要是理所当然的，因为人力资本是你最重要的资产。然而，这件事不会有什么大张旗鼓的公告，你不可能发一份新闻稿说“哦，我的员工非常投入”。所以我考察的是“美国最佳雇主 100 强”榜单。

turns.en: Those are companies that go above and beyond and how they treat their employees. And over 28 year period, these companies beat their peers by 2.3 to 3.8% per year. That's 89 to 184% compounded. Now this is public information, so it should be that as soon as you get added to the list, the stock price should jump, but the market didn't.
turns.zh: 榜上的都是那些在对待员工方面远超同行的公司。在 28 年的时间跨度里，这些公司每年跑赢同行 2.3% 到 3.8%，复利下来是 89% 到 184%。这属于公开信息，所以按理说，一家公司一被加入榜单，股价就应该跳涨，但市场没有。

turns.en: It ignored information hiding in plain sight. Why number one is that there's not a big huge public announcement like there is with earnings. turns.zh: 市场忽略了就摆在明面上的信息。原因第一，它不像财报那样有重大的公开公告。第二，也许有些人认为，一家对员工友好的公司是“觉醒派”（woke）、是抱树环保派，它并不专注于底线，也就是创造利润和股息。

turns.en: Third reason is even if you knew that employees are happy and you know that that is a good thing, you might not know what to do with that information. So with quantitative information, you know what to do about it. If indeed earnings are 5% higher than previously, maybe you can increase every sell in your spreadsheet by 5%.
turns.zh: 第三个原因是，即便你知道员工很满意，也知道这是好事，你未必知道该怎么用这个信息。对于量化信息，你知道该怎么处理：如果盈利确实比原先高出 5%，也许你可以把电子表格里的每一项销售预测都上调 5%。

turns.en: But if you know that your employees are happy, it's hard to know how to change sell C23 in your spreadsheet, so maybe people might just actually not do anything about it. They overreact sometimes, they underreact sometimes. Do investors ever just react incorrectly to information?
turns.zh: 但如果你只知道员工很开心，你就很难知道该怎么改电子表格里 C23 那个单元格，所以人们也许干脆什么都不做。他们有时过度反应，有时反应不足。那投资者会不会对信息做出纯粹错误的反应呢？

turns.en: Yeah, so also investors will misreact, so they will make mistakes, which have no direction attached to them. So one example is they will anchor too much on the purchase price even though that's not relevant. So what determines how you should trade now is the current price of the stock versus what
turns.zh: 会的，投资者也会误反应，也就是犯一些没有方向性的错误。一个例子是，他们会过度锚定（anchoring）于买入价格，尽管那并不相关。决定你现在该如何交易的，是股票的当前价格与你

turns.en: you think the current value is, but instead people think about what they bought it at and that will be an anchor. So maybe that if you bought the stock at 100 and it's at 120 now, then you're on profit. People want to take profit so they're more likely to sell.
turns.zh: 认为的当前价值之间的对比，但人们想的却是自己当初买在什么价位，那会成为一个锚。所以，如果你在 100 买入，现在到了 120，你就是浮盈状态。人们想落袋为安，所以更可能卖出。

turns.en: In contrast, if they bought it at 100 and it went down to 80, then they're sitting on a loss and they don't want to sell because it's really difficult to take a loss. turns.zh: 相反，如果你在 100 买入，跌到了 80，你就处于浮亏，你不愿意卖，因为承认亏损实在太难了。于是你会看到这样一个问题：人们急于兑现赢家，却死抱着输家不放。

turns.en: Even though you should actually do the opposite because in the short term, what you typically see is under reaction. And so a stock which has done well recently continues to do well, a stock that has done badly recently continues to do badly. But if we anchor too much on the purchase price and focus too much on how is it done
turns.zh: 尽管你其实应该做相反的事，因为在短期内你通常看到的是反应不足：最近表现好的股票会继续表现好，最近表现差的股票会继续表现差。但如果我们过度锚定于买入价，过度关注我们买入之后它表现如何，

turns.en: since we bought it, then we're actually anchoring on something which is not relevant. What drives investors swings from Zuberance to panic? So again, this will be over reaction. So it will be that if you have a lot of, say, excitement about tech and then you see
turns.zh: 那我们其实是在锚定一个不相关的东西。是什么导致投资者从亢奋摆向恐慌？这同样是过度反应。也就是说，如果大家对科技股非常兴奋，然后突然

turns.en: oh, well, actually we believe that tech is problematic now or there could be some issue with people overspending, then it may be all be that people overracked. So just as we've discussed over action and many other areas over action will cause people to latch on to small bits of information and make much more of this than they actually
turns.zh: 觉得“哦，其实我们现在认为科技股有问题了”，或者出现某些人过度支出的问题，那可能全都是过度反应的结果。就像我们在许多其他领域讨论过的过度反应一样，过度反应会让人们抓住一点点信息，并且把它放大到远超其

turns.en: should. How does value investing exploit the same over reaction? This is interesting because this is another way into exploiting over reactions. So what I discussed earlier is looking at the past three year stock price performance buying the loses and selling the winners.
turns.zh: 应有的程度。价值投资是如何利用同样的过度反应的？这很有意思，因为这是利用过度反应的另一条路径。我之前讲的是看过去三年的股价表现，买入输家、卖出赢家。

turns.en: But the other thing that you can do is you can look at a valuation multiple. And that is what value investing is about. So what is a valuation multiple? Let's think about how you value a house. You might compare the price of a house to the size. So you look at the price per square meter.
turns.zh: 但你还可以做另一件事：看估值倍数（valuation multiple）。而这正是价值投资的核心。那么什么是估值倍数？想想你是怎么给房子估值的。你可能会把房价和面积做比较，也就是看每平方米的价格，

turns.en: And you might compare that to other houses in the same neighborhood. And if one house is as a much higher price per square meter than the others, then it may will be over priced unless it happens to be in a much better condition. And so this is what you will do with stock.
turns.zh: 然后跟同一社区的其他房子做对比。如果某套房子的每平方米价格远高于其他房子，那它可能被高估了，除非它的状况确实好得多。对股票你也会做同样的事。

turns.en: So rather than price per square meter, what you might look at is the price to earnings ratio. So this is the price of a stock compared to the earnings per share. turns.zh: 所以，你看的不是每平方米价格，而是市盈率（price-to-earnings ratio）。也就是股价与每股收益的比较，每股收益代表的是一家公司的基本面价值。如果同一行业、同一成熟度阶段的公司中，有一家的

turns.zh: 市盈率远高于另一家，那你很可能会认为它被高估了。举个 2000 年的例子：思科（Cisco）的市盈率是 190 倍，是微软的三倍、英特尔的四倍。是的，那是科技股的辉煌年份，但即便如此，思科也不应该远高于同行。

turns.zh: 问一句：我们谈的这些策略——价值、反转，还有一些稍后会谈到的——为什么在公开发表之后不会失效？这一点非常重要，因为我听起来像是描述了一个对投资者来说极其简单的策略：

turns.en: for investors, you just buy past losers or you buy stocks with low price earnings ratios and you magically sit back and then wait for the money to roll in. turns.zh: 你只要买入过去的输家，或者买入低市盈率的股票，然后神奇地坐在那里等钱滚滚而来。如果真这么简单，为什么聪明的投资者不这么做呢？原因在于现实世界中会出问题。我来举个例子。

turns.en: So in late 1999, many people thought there was a tech bubble based on the multiples, like 190 for Cisco, this seems crazy. And so Julian Robertson was a very smart investor here and tiger asset management. And he thought we'll let short this tech bubble. And so he did.
turns.zh: 1999 年底，很多人根据估值倍数判断存在科技泡沫，比如思科 190 倍的市盈率，这看起来太疯狂了。朱利安·罗伯逊（Julian Robertson）是一位非常聪明的投资者，他在老虎资产管理公司（Tiger Asset Management）。他想：好，我们来做空这个科技泡沫。于是他做了。

turns.zh: 你随便说点什么，他就知道是哪篇论文，知道它什么时候发表，知道论文里到底说了什么。天哪，这太了不起了。和他聊这些东西非常有意思。我想起我听大卫·奇尔顿（David Chilton）的播客《富有的理发师》（The Wealthy Barber），他谈到……
